# Middle_ages claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 789 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 932 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (932 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/middle_ages.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

- **Source:** `source.beauvais_cathedral_history`

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.gothic_beauvais_collapse_1284`: unverified

> **Claim:** In November 1284 Beauvais's flying buttresses twisted and broke and the choir vault collapsed, probably triggered by a storm; rebuilding took until about 1340.

- **Concept:** Gothic engineering (`concept.middle_ages.gothic_cathedral_engineering`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Building Cathedrals” · `card.middle_ages.033.c4` (text): When the ceiling fell / At Beauvais, builders raised the tallest Gothic stone vault in the world. In November 1284 its flying buttresses twisted and broke, and the choir vault came down, probably set off by a storm. Rebuilding took until about 1340. Gothic builders were pushing stone to its limits, and sometimes the stone pushed back.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia Beauvais Cathedral and CTBUH paper: the choir vault and several flying buttresses collapsed in 1284, likely from wind-induced vibration; it was rebuilt with extra supports. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauvais_Cathedral, https://global.ctbuh.org/resources/papers/download/1748-the-analysis-on-the-collapse-of-the-tallest-gothic-cathedral.pdf

## Bloodletting and leeches, not so ancient (British Library)

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.humours_balance`: unverified

> **Claim:** In humoral theory the ideal person had a balanced mixture of the four humours, and illness came from an imbalance.

- **Concept:** The four humours (`concept.middle_ages.four_humours_theory`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L57 “Medicine and the Four Humors” · `card.middle_ages.057.c2` (text): Four liquids in balance / The theory was ancient. Hippocrates championed it, and Galen, Rome’s leading medical authority in the 2nd century CE, built on it; it was still current throughout the Middle Ages. The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy). The ideal person had them perfectly balanced, and illness meant one had got out of proportion. Health was a recipe, and sickness meant too much of one ingredient.
- **Tested by:**
  - L57 `question.middle_ages.057.q1`: Which four humours did medieval medicine believe governed the body? → **Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: "The ideal person had the ideally proportioned mixture of the four". British Library: health and disease occurred when the humours were imbalanced. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/humor-ancient-physiology, https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/bloodletting-and-leeches-not-so-ancient

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.humours_remove_excess`: unverified

> **Claim:** To cure illness, healers tried to remove the excess humour, for example by letting blood or applying leeches.

- **Concept:** Diagnosis and bloodletting (`concept.middle_ages.humoral_treatment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L57 “Medicine and the Four Humors” · `card.middle_ages.057.c4` (text): Letting out the excess / If one humour was in excess, healers tried to remove it, by letting blood or applying leeches. After a church edict of 1163 barred clergy from bloodletting, barber-surgeons took it up alongside shaving and pulling teeth, a legacy you can still see in the barber’s pole. Bloodletting lost credibility in the 18th and 19th centuries, when studies showed it worked less well than claimed. / This is the history of an idea, not medical advice

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. British Library: to remedy illness practitioners removed "the excess of the relevant humor", including with leeches. Britannica: by the Middle Ages bloodletting had become standard treatment. Sources: https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/bloodletting-and-leeches-not-so-ancient, https://www.britannica.com/science/bloodletting

## Shameful and Demeaning: The Annulment of Magna Carta (The British Library)

- **Source:** `source.bl_magna_carta_annulment`
- **URL:** https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/shameful-and-demeaning-the-annulment-of-magna-carta
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.magna_carta_annulled`: unverified

> **Claim:** On 24 August 1215, less than ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III, to whom John had submitted his kingdom, annulled Magna Carta as "shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust".

- **Concept:** Magna Carta's survival (`concept.middle_ages.magna_carta_survival`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Magna Carta” · `card.middle_ages.071.c1` (text): In June 1215 a king agreed to a charter. By August, the Pope had killed it. / Magna Carta, the “Great Charter”, was dead in less than ten weeks. So why does anyone still care about it? Because it refused to stay dead.
  - L71 “Magna Carta” · `card.middle_ages.071.c3` (text): Dead in ten weeks / It didn’t last. John had submitted his kingdom to the Pope, so he appealed to him. On 24 August 1215, less than ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III annulled the charter, calling it “shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust”. Fighting broke out again in September and went on until John died in October 1216. As peace deals go, it was a flop.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Kings, Parliaments and Law” · `card.middle_ages.080.c3` (text): The charter that wouldn’t die / Remember Level 71’s flop, annulled within ten weeks? Kings kept confirming it: modern research counts as many as 44 reaffirmations, the last in 1423. In 1297 it was recorded in the Statute Rolls for the first time. By the 14th century, Parliament’s regular reconfirmations were a public reminder that the king had to uphold the rule of law. The king still ruled. He just no longer ruled alone.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. House of Commons Library: within 10 weeks of being sealed in 1215 it was annulled by Pope Innocent III; National Archives timeline: papal bulls of 24-25 August 1215 declare it null and void. Sources: https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/magna-carta-does-it-still-matter/, https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/teaching-resources/magna-carta-1214-1225/


The Anglo-Saxons ruled until the Norman Conquest of 1066.

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.copying_needed`: unverified

> **Claim:** Monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, which meant much time spent copying manuscripts.

- **Concept:** Monks and books (`concept.middle_ages.monastic_copying`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Monasteries” · `card.middle_ages.007.c3` (text): Why monks copied / Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. But monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, and the only way to get a book was to copy one. So monasteries set aside a writing room, the scriptorium, where scribes copied manuscripts onto parchment or vellum, made from animal skin. No printer, no photocopier: just a pen and a very long afternoon.
- **Tested by:**
  - L7 `question.middle_ages.007.q2`: Why did early medieval monasteries copy so many books? → **Monks needed Bibles and service books, and copying was the only way**
  - L10 `question.middle_ages.010.q4`: In the early medieval West, where were most books copied? → **In monastery writing rooms, the scriptoria**
  - L13 `question.middle_ages.013.q3`: Level 7’s monasteries were storehouses of books. Why did Viking raiders target them? → **They held silver and were poorly defended**
  - L37 `question.middle_ages.037.q3`: Before 1476, how did copies of Sacrobosco’s Sphere reach students across Europe? → **Copied out by hand, as manuscripts**
  - L65 `question.middle_ages.065.q3`: Level 7’s monks wrote on parchment made from animal skin. What did Chinese craftsmen first make paper from? → **Washed rags dried on a screen**
  - L100 `question.middle_ages.100.q2`: Renaissance humanists called the Middle Ages dark. What irony did Poggio’s book hunts reveal? → **The classics they loved survived in medieval monks’ copies**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Viva Pressbooks, Early Medieval Manuscripts: monks copied Bibles and liturgical books for monastic use. Sources: https://viva.pressbooks.pub/arthistory/chapter/early-medieval-manuscripts/

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.rule_balance`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Rule of St. Benedict balanced prayer, work and study, with about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, plus enough food and sleep.

- **Concept:** Benedict's Rule (`concept.middle_ages.benedictine_rule`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Monasteries” · `card.middle_ages.007.c2` (text): A rule for living / In 529 Benedict of Nursia founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy. He wrote a Rule for it that balanced prayer, work and study: about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, with enough food and sleep. Moderate, as monastic life goes. By the early 9th century his Rule had replaced most others across northern and western Europe. One man’s timetable became a continent’s.
  - L35 “Monks and Nuns” · `card.middle_ages.035.c2` (text): The Divine Office / The backbone of the day was the Divine Office: psalms, hymns, prayers and readings at set hours. Matins, the longest, came at night. Prime came early, lauds and vespers were the great morning and evening prayers, terce, sext and none marked mid-morning, noon and mid-afternoon, and compline was the night prayer. Remember Benedict’s balance of prayer, work and reading? The Office was the prayer. The work and study fitted in between.

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.plague_jews_blamed`: unverified

> **Claim:** Jews were falsely accused of causing the Black Death by poisoning wells, and many were killed by mobs or burned.

- **Concept:** Faith, fear and blame (`concept.middle_ages.plague_faith_fear`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L84 “A World Changed by Plague” · `card.middle_ages.084.c5` (text): The search for someone to blame / Fear also turned to murder. Jews were falsely accused of causing the plague by poisoning wells, and across Europe many were killed by mobs or burned. In Strasbourg, on 14 February 1349, about 2,000 Jews were burned, a city chronicler recorded. The plague only reached Strasbourg that summer. Jews were dying of the plague too, yet the accusation was widely believed. At Avignon, Pope Clement VI protected them.

> **Claim:** From Caffa, Genoese ships carried the plague west to Mediterranean ports.

- **Concept:** How the Black Death reached Europe (`concept.middle_ages.black_death_arrival`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “The Black Death Arrives” · `card.middle_ages.082.c2` (text): It began far to the east / The trail starts in Central Asia. Near Lake Issyk-Kul, in today’s Kyrgyzstan, graves with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 held plague DNA, pointing there as the source. By 1346 it had reached Crimea, where a Mongol army besieging the Italian trading port of Caffa began to die of it. ### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.vellum`: unverified

> **Claim:** Medieval books were written on parchment or vellum, prepared from animal skin.

- **Concept:** Monks and books (`concept.middle_ages.monastic_copying`)

  - L7 “Monasteries” · `card.middle_ages.007.c3` (text): Why monks copied / Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. But monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, and the only way to get a book was to copy one. So monasteries set aside a writing room, the scriptorium, where scribes copied manuscripts onto parchment or vellum, made from animal skin. No printer, no photocopier: just a pen and a very long afternoon.
  - L65 “Paper and Books” · `card.middle_ages.065.c4` (text): Baghdad’s paper, Europe’s turn / Paper was being made in Baghdad by the 790s, under the caliph Harun al-Rashid, and soon scholars across the Islamic world were copying manuscripts onto it. Remember Level 7’s monks, writing on parchment or vellum made from animal skin? Paper came from rags instead. It reached Europe through Sicily and Spain by the 12th century. Old shirts in, libraries out.
  - L91 “The Printing Press” · `card.middle_ages.091.c3` (text): Borrowed from the wine press / To press ink onto a page firmly and evenly, Gutenberg built a press, probably adapted from the ones used for wine, oil or paper. His showpiece, the 42-line Bible, came off it in Mainz around 1455, in a run of perhaps as many as 180 copies. About a quarter were printed on vellum, the same animal skin the monks of Level 7 wrote on. Old material, new machine.

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.manor_demesne`: unverified

> **Claim:** The demesne was the part of a manor the lord kept for his own use, and serfs supplied the labour to work it.

- **Concept:** What peasants owed the manor (`concept.middle_ages.manor_obligations`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Serfs and Peasants” · `card.middle_ages.022.c3` (text): Working the lord’s land / Every manor had a demesne, the part the lord kept for his own use, and serfs supplied the labour to work it. Week by week an unfree peasant, a villein, brought his own plough and oxen to plough the demesne, then harrowed, reaped, threshed and carried the crops. This duty was called week-work. His own holding, a cottage and some strips of land in the fields, had to fit around it. Picture paying your rent by doing your landlord’s gardening every single week.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Castles and Knights” · `card.middle_ages.030.c3` (text): Pray, fight, work / In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Like chivalry, it was an ideal, but a medieval one, unlike the modern pyramid. It maps this chapter well. Many knights held land as fiefs and fought for their lords. Serfs worked the lord’s demesne every week. And castles, the homes of kings and lords, held the land together. Fighters, workers, and the stone that kept them in place.
- **Tested by:**
  - L22 `question.middle_ages.022.q2`: What was week-work on a medieval manor? → **Regular labour on the lord’s demesne**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. olemiss Manorial Language: demesne is the part of the lord's lands reserved for his own use; Britannica History of Europe: serfs supplied the labour needed to work the demesne. Sources: https://home.olemiss.edu/~tjray/medieval/manorial.htm, https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Europe/Landlords-and-peasants

  - L7 “Monasteries” · `card.middle_ages.007.c3` (text): Why monks copied / Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. > **Claim:** Eyeglasses were first made in Italy, most probably in Pisa, around 1290; the first ones had convex lenses to help farsighted people.

  - L99 “What the Middle Ages Left Us” · `card.middle_ages.099.c1` (text): If you wear glasses, you’re wearing a medieval invention. / The Middle Ages ended, but they never quite left. Some of what they made is on your face, on your wall and in the law.
  - L99 “What the Middle Ages Left Us” · `card.middle_ages.099.c2` (text): A friar remembers / Eyeglasses were first made in Italy, most probably in Pisa, around 1290; the first ones helped farsighted people read. How do we know the date? In a sermon of 1306, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making them was not yet twenty years old, and that he had talked to the man who discovered it. The inventor’s name is lost. The invention is not.

## Fashion for pointy shoes unleashed a plague of bunions in medieval Britain (University of Cambridge)

- **Source:** `source.cam_pointy_shoes_bunions`
- **URL:** https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/bunions
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.clothes_bunions`: unverified

> **Claim:** Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th, and linked the rise to pointed shoes.

- **Concept:** Cloth as a badge of rank (`concept.middle_ages.clothing_status`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L55 “Clothes and Status” · `card.middle_ages.055.c4` (text): The pointy-shoe problem / Late-medieval fashion loved poulaines, shoes with long pointed toes. In 1463 King Edward IV limited the points in London to under two inches. The fashion left marks you can still measure: Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries, but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th. The bones kept the receipts.
- **Tested by:**
  - L55 `question.middle_ages.055.q2`: Why do Cambridge researchers link a rise in medieval bunions to fashion? → **Bunions rose as pointed shoes came into style**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. University of Cambridge: 6% of individuals from the 11th-13th centuries versus 27% from the 14th-15th centuries, linked to pointed-toe shoes. Smithsonian Magazine reports the same figures. Sources: https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/bunions, https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/medieval-europeans-obsession-pointy-shoes-caused-painful-bunions-180977969/

## Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa (Mark Wheelis) (Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC))

- **Source:** `source.cdc_eid_caffa_siege`
- **URL:** https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/8/9/01-0536_article

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.black_death_caffa_1346`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1346 a Mongol army under Janibeg besieging Caffa, an Italian trading port in Crimea, was struck by plague.

- **Concept:** How the Black Death reached Europe (`concept.middle_ages.black_death_arrival`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “The Black Death Arrives” · `card.middle_ages.082.c2` (text): It began far to the east / The trail starts in Central Asia. Near Lake Issyk-Kul, in today’s Kyrgyzstan, graves with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 held plague DNA, pointing there as the source. By 1346 it had reached Crimea, where a Mongol army besieging the Italian trading port of Caffa began to die of it. One chronicler claimed the besiegers catapulted corpses over the walls, though he probably wasn’t there to see it. Genoese ships then carried the plague west.
  - L82 “The Black Death Arrives” · `card.middle_ages.082.c3` (timeline): Across Europe, year by year: 1338–1339: Plague deaths near Lake Issyk-Kul, Central Asia; 1346: Plague strikes the siege of Caffa, in Crimea; October 1347: Ships bring it to Messina, in Sicily; 1348: Italy, Spain and France; 1349: Germany and the Low Countries; 1350: Scandinavia and the Baltic
- **Tested by:**
  - L82 `question.middle_ages.082.q1`: In October 1347, where did ships bring the Black Death ashore? → **Messina, in Sicily**
  - L82 `question.middle_ages.082.q3`: What linked the plague at the siege of Caffa to its arrival in Sicily? → **Genoese ships carried it west across the sea**
  - L83 `question.middle_ages.083.q3`: The Black Death travelled by ship from Crimea. Which form of plague could pass directly from sailor to sailor? → **Pneumonic plague, through respiratory droplets**
  - L90 `question.middle_ages.090.q1`: Plague and war: which of these came in the right order? → **The Great Famine, the Black Death reaches Messina, the Peasants’ Revolt**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: the Black Death decimated the army of the Kipchak khan Janibeg while he was besieging the Genoese port of Kaffa in Crimea. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/event/Black-Death/Cause-and-outbreak
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

> **Claim:** Constantinople's land walls, begun under Emperor Theodosius II in 412, combined a moat, an outer wall and a main wall with 96 towers.

- **Concept:** How Byzantium lasted (`concept.middle_ages.byzantine_survival`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Byzantine Empire” · `card.middle_ages.004.c3` (text): Three walls deep / Constantinople’s best defense was its land walls, begun under Emperor Theodosius II in 412. An attacker faced a moat, then an outer wall, then a taller main wall studded with 96 towers. Those walls held firm through the early Middle Ages against Germanic, Hun, Avar, Slav and Arab attackers. The city fell only in 1453, to Ottoman forces armed with heavy cannon. Attackers had to win three times in a row; defenders only had to win once.
  - L24 “Castle Defenses” · `card.middle_ages.024.c4` (text): Walls within walls / The most powerful design was the concentric castle: two rings of towered walls, one inside the other, each supporting the other. At Beaumaris in Wales, Edward I and his architect James of St George built four rings of defences, including a water-filled moat with its own dock. The outer walls alone had 300 arrow loops. Then the money ran out, and work petered out by the 1320s, unfinished. Remember Constantinople’s moat and layered walls in Level 4? Same idea: make attackers win again and again.
  - L87 “The Fall of Constantinople” · `card.middle_ages.087.c1` (text): Level 4’s land walls had stood since 412. In 1453 a young sultan brought cannon. / His name was Mehmed II, and he was 21. How did he take the city nobody could take?

  - L24 `question.middle_ages.024.q3`: Beaumaris and Level 4’s Constantinople shared which defensive idea? → **Layers of walls that attackers had to break in turn**
  - L47 `question.middle_ages.047.q3`: Level 4’s walls held Constantinople through the early Middle Ages. How did the crusaders get in on 12 April 1204? → **They climbed onto the walls from ships**

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.feudal_pyramid_simplification`: unverified

> **Claim:** The tidy feudal pyramid is a simplification: relations between kings, lords, knights and peasants differed widely across medieval Europe.

- **Concept:** Feudalism: a debated label (`concept.middle_ages.feudal_label_debate`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L21 “Feudalism” · `card.middle_ages.021.c4` (text): Handle the pyramid with care / You may have seen it drawn as a pyramid: king on top, then lords, knights and peasants. Treat that as a simplification, because arrangements differed widely across Europe. In 1974 the historian Elizabeth A. R. Brown argued that feudalism has no agreed definition and is misleading. In 1994 Susan Reynolds argued that words like fief and vassal had no precise technical meaning until lawyers defined them in the late 12th century. Many historians now avoid the term.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia Feudalism: the pyramid concept dates to Whitaker (1771); Brown called the term an anachronism imparting a false sense of uniformity. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.jury_after_1215`: unverified

> **Claim:** After the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 withdrew priests from trials by ordeal, England turned to juries to decide guilt, building on its existing jury of presentment.

- **Concept:** The first juries (`concept.middle_ages.jury_origins`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L73 “Common Law and Juries” · `card.middle_ages.073.c1` (text): The first English juries didn’t decide who was guilty. They named suspects. / Under Henry II, twelve local men were the king’s informers. How did a jury go from pointing fingers to deciding cases? The answer runs through 1215.
  - L73 “Common Law and Juries” · `card.middle_ages.073.c4` (text): From accusers to deciders / Then, in 1215, the Church pulled its priests out of trials by ordeal (Level 74 has the gory details). England needed a new way to settle guilt, and it had a group of sworn neighbours ready: the jury. Soon juries were deciding guilt as well. On the continent, Level 5’s Justinian code became the root of civil law. England went its own way, and its common law later spread to the United States and most of the Commonwealth.
  - L74 “Trial by Ordeal” · `card.middle_ages.074.c5` (text): The end of the ordeal / An ordeal needed a priest to bless the iron or the water. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade that blessing, and in England the ordeal soon came to an end. Remember Level 73? The jury stepped in to decide guilt. Without God’s test, people had to weigh the evidence themselves.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia Trial by ordeal and Assize of Clarendon: after the 1215 ban on clerical participation, trial by ordeal ended in England and trial by jury replaced it. Around 1230 Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at Paris, wrote The Sphere, which became the most popular university astronomy textbook. It argued at length that the Earth is round. ## Origins of the Black Death identified (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft)

- **Source:** `source.mpg_black_death_origins`
- **URL:** https://www.mpg.de/18778852/0607-evan-origins-of-the-black-death-identified-150495-x
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.black_death_central_asia`: unverified

> **Claim:** Plague DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339, points to Central Asia as the Black Death's source.

- **Concept:** How the Black Death reached Europe (`concept.middle_ages.black_death_arrival`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “The Black Death Arrives” · `card.middle_ages.082.c2` (text): It began far to the east / The trail starts in Central Asia. Near Lake Issyk-Kul, in today’s Kyrgyzstan, graves with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 held plague DNA, pointing there as the source. By 1346 it had reached Crimea, where a Mongol army besieging the Italian trading port of Caffa began to die of it. One chronicler claimed the besiegers catapulted corpses over the walls, though he probably wasn’t there to see it. Genoese ships then carried the plague west.
  - L82 “The Black Death Arrives” · `card.middle_ages.082.c3` (timeline): Across Europe, year by year: 1338–1339: Plague deaths near Lake Issyk-Kul, Central Asia; 1346: Plague strikes the siege of Caffa, in Crimea; October 1347: Ships bring it to Messina, in Sicily; 1348: Italy, Spain and France; 1349: Germany and the Low Countries; 1350: Scandinavia and the Baltic
- **Tested by:**
  - L82 `question.middle_ages.082.q1`: In October 1347, where did ships bring the Black Death ashore? → **Messina, in Sicily**
  - L82 `question.middle_ages.082.q3`: What linked the plague at the siege of Caffa to its arrival in Sicily? → **Genoese ships carried it west across the sea**
  - L83 `question.middle_ages.083.q3`: The Black Death travelled by ship from Crimea. Which form of plague could pass directly from sailor to sailor? → **Pneumonic plague, through respiratory droplets**
  - L90 `question.middle_ages.090.q1`: Plague and war: which of these came in the right order? → **The Great Famine, the Black Death reaches Messina, the Peasants’ Revolt**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDaily and Science (AAAS) report the 2022 Nature study: burials spiked in 1338-1339 near Issyk-Kul, three of seven individuals tested positive for Y. pestis at the root of the Black Death strains. Sources: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/06/220615113242.htm, https://www.science.org/content/article/800-year-old-graves-pinpoint-where-black-death-began

## Maybe Rats Aren't to Blame for the Black Death (National Geographic)

- **Source:** `source.natgeo_rats_black_death`

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.plague_dean_2018`: unverified

> **Claim:** A 2018 study led by Katharine Dean found that human fleas and body lice fit the death records better than rats in seven of nine European plague outbreaks from 1348 to 1813.

- **Concept:** Rats or people? The transmission debate (`concept.middle_ages.plague_transmission_debate`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L83 “How the Plague Spread” · `card.middle_ages.083.c4` (text): Rats on trial / The textbook story blames rats: infected fleas jump from rodents to people, which is how plague spreads today. In 2018 a team led by Katharine Dean tested that story against death records from nine European outbreaks, from 1348 to 1813. In seven of the nine, a model where human fleas and body lice passed plague between people fit the records better than rats did. Other historians disagree, and the debate is still open. The rat isn’t acquitted. It just has company.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Phys.org (University of Oslo study): the human ectoparasite model fit mortality curves from nine outbreaks between 1348 and 1813 better than rodent models; CBC reports the same. Sources: https://phys.org/news/2018-01-human-fleas-lice-black-death.html, https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/black-death-fleas-lice-1.4485664

- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Magna Carta” · `card.middle_ages.071.c1` (text): In June 1215 a king agreed to a charter. By August, the Pope had killed it. / Magna Carta, the “Great Charter”, was dead in less than ten weeks. So why does anyone still care about it? Because it refused to stay dead.

> **Claim:** Medieval scholars knew the Earth is a sphere; the idea that medieval people thought it flat is a myth spread by 19th-century writers.

  - L37 “The First Universities” · `card.middle_ages.037.c4` (text): A round Earth on the syllabus / One thing they taught: the Earth is a sphere. Around 1230 Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at Paris, wrote The Sphere, which became the most popular university astronomy textbook. It argued at length that the Earth is round. ### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.three_orders`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work.

- **Appears in:**
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Castles and Knights” · `card.middle_ages.030.c1` (text): Chapter 3 finale: a medieval bishop sorted society into three kinds of people. / Those who pray, those who fight and those who work. You’ve just spent a chapter with two of them. Let’s put land, castles and knights on one page.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Castles and Knights” · `card.middle_ages.030.c3` (text): Pray, fight, work / In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Like chivalry, it was an ideal, but a medieval one, unlike the modern pyramid. It maps this chapter well. Many knights held land as fiefs and fought for their lords. Serfs worked the lord’s demesne every week. And castles, the homes of kings and lords, held the land together. Fighters, workers, and the stone that kept them in place.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Medievalists.net: in the 1020s Adalbero of Laon and Gerard of Cambrai independently described society as those who fought, laboured and prayed. Sources: https://www.medievalists.net/2023/11/three-orders-medieval-society/, https://www.medievalists.net/2025/03/historiography-feudalism-medieval-historian/

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.chivalry_prowess`: unverified

> **Claim:** In chivalric writing, prowess, skill at violent deeds, became almost a one-word definition of chivalry.

- **Concept:** Chivalry in practice (`concept.middle_ages.chivalry_reality`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L28 “Chivalry” · `card.middle_ages.028.c4` (text): Part of the problem / Some historians go further. In 1999 Richard Kaeuper argued that chivalry was part of the problem of violence in medieval Europe, not merely its solution. Chivalric writing prized prowess, skill at violent deeds, so highly that it became almost a one-word definition of chivalry, even as the Church tried to regulate knightly violence. The code was real. So was the gap.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OUP and Semantic Scholar summaries of Kaeuper: chivalry praised heroic violence and fused prowess with honour and piety. Sources: https://global.oup.com/academic/product/chivalry-and-violence-in-medieval-europe-9780199244584, https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Chivalry-and-violence-in-medieval-Europe-Kaeuper/0ce2781980688d36e3790b3fa511146cb9ea6e0b

### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.domesday_pig`: unverified

> **Claim:** A writer of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complained that not one ox, cow or pig was left out of William's record.

- **Concept:** The Domesday Book (`concept.middle_ages.domesday_survey`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L19 “The Domesday Book” · `card.middle_ages.019.c1` (text): Nineteen years after Hastings, William wanted to count every pig in England. / Or so it felt to the English. The result names more than 13,000 places, and most of them still exist.
  - L19 “The Domesday Book” · `card.middle_ages.019.c3` (text): Who? How many? What’s it worth? / Commissioners asked the same questions everywhere. Who held this manor under King Edward, and who holds it now? How many plough teams and mills? What was it worth in 1066, and what now? The answers showed how England had changed since the Conquest. One writer of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complained that not one ox, cow or pig was left out. Picture a tax inspector with a clipboard, times a whole kingdom.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Charlemagne and the Vikings” · `card.middle_ages.020.c3` (text): Raiders, then rulers / Einhard wrote that Charlemagne built a fleet against the Northmen and posted guards at harbours and river mouths, because they kept raiding the coasts. The Vikings kept coming anyway. In England, Alfred beat them at Edington, then shared the land with the Danelaw. In France, the king gave Rollo Normandy. And William the Conqueror, Rollo’s great-great-great-grandson, took England in 1066 and then counted its pigs. The Vikings didn’t only raid Europe. Their descendants ended up running part of it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L19 `question.middle_ages.019.q3`: Domesday compared each manor’s worth in 1066 and in 1086. Why start from 1066? → **It was the year of the Norman Conquest**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Medieval genealogy guide to Domesday: the Chronicle says not 'one ox nor one cow nor one pig' was omitted. Sources: https://www.medievalgenealogy.org.uk/guide/dom.shtml
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

> **Claim:** After John's death the charter was reissued in the name of his young son, Henry III, in 1216 and 1217, and again in 1225 in exchange for a new tax.

After John’s death the charter was reissued in the name of his young son, Henry III, in 1216 and again in 1217. In 1225 it came back once more, this time in exchange for a new tax. The failed peace deal had become a bargain: rights for money. And pieces of it are still here. Three clauses remain in English law today: the freedom of the English Church, the ancient liberties of the City of London, and the right to lawful judgment. / Three clauses of Magna Carta are still English law
  - L72 “The First Parliaments” · `card.middle_ages.072.c3` (text): Money talks / Here’s why they caught on. Wars cost more than a king could pay from his own wealth. ### ☐ `fact.middle_ages.magna_carta_clause_39`: unverified

Its most famous promise, clause 39: no free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land. Clause 40 added that the king would not sell, deny or delay justice to anyone. In short: the king can’t just lock you up.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Reviews of Freedman's Out of the East: he calls the spoiled-meat idea a false urban legend; the price of spices far exceeded that of fresh meat, and salting, pickling or smoking preserved better. Medievalists.net: spices were far too expensive to waste on bad meat.
